q: How many blood group systems have been defined based on antigens located on the surfaces of red blood cells?
e: Twenty five blood group systems have been defined on the bases of antigens located on the surfaces of red blood cells.

q: Who discovered the ABO blood group system?
e: Discovery of the ABO system by the Austrian Karl Landsteiner in 1901 marked the beginning of safe blood transfusion.

q: In what year was the ABO blood system discovered?
e: The ABO system was discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1901.

q: Which two blood group systems are of key importance in determining the compatibility of blood transfusions?
e: The ABO- system and RH- systems are both of key importance in determining the compatibility of blood transfusions.

q: What determines a blood group system genetically?
o: A single genetic locus or very closely linked loci
e: Each system is a series of red cell antigens determined by either a single genetic locus or very closely linked loci.

q: Which antigen is present on the surface of red blood cells in a blood group A individual?
e: Individuals with blood group A have the A antigen on the surface of their RBCs.

q: Which antibodies are found in the blood serum of a group A individual?
e: Blood group A individuals have blood serum containing Anti-B antibodies.

q: From which blood groups can a group A individual safely receive blood?
e: A group A individual can only receive blood from individuals of groups A or O.

q: To which blood groups can a group A individual donate blood?
e: A group A individual can donate blood to individuals of groups A or AB.

q: Which antigen is present on the surface of red blood cells in a blood group B individual?
e: Individuals with blood group B have the B antigen on their surface of their RBCs.

q: What antibodies are present in the blood serum of a group B individual?
e: Group B individuals have blood serum containing Anti-A antibodies.

q: Which blood groups can donate blood to a group B individual?
e: A group B individual can only receive blood from individuals of groups B or O.

q: What antigens are found on the red blood cells of an individual with blood group AB?
e: Individuals with blood group AB have both A and B antigens on the surface of their RBCs.

q: Which antibodies exist in the serum of a person with type AB blood?
e: Their blood serum does not contain any antibodies against either A or B antigen.

q: Which blood group is known as the 'Universal Recipient'?
e: Type AB individuals are universal recipients because they can receive blood from any group.

q: To whom can an individual with type AB blood donate?
e: An individual with type AB blood can only donate blood to another group AB individual.

q: Which antigens are on the surface of red blood cells in a group O individual?
e: Group O individuals do not have either A or B antigens on the surface of their RBCs.

q: What antibodies are present in the serum of a group O individual?
e: Group O blood serum contains both Anti-A and Anti-B antibodies.

q: Which blood type is considered the 'Universal Donor'?
e: Group O individuals can donate blood to any ABO blood group (A, B, O, or AB), making them universal donors.

q: From which blood group can a type O individual receive a blood transfusion?
e: A group O individual can only receive blood from a group O individual.

q: How many genes control the ABO blood type?
e: The ABO blood type is controlled by a single gene.

q: On which chromosome is the gene responsible for the ABO blood group located?
e: The gene is located on chromosome 9.

q: How many alleles does the gene responsible for ABO blood groups have?
e: It has 3 alleles: IA, IB, and I°.

q: What type of enzyme does the ABO gene encode?
e: The gene encodes a glycosyltransferase enzyme.

q: An individual with the IAIB genotype will express which blood type?
e: Those with both alleles express both antigens, resulting in blood type AB.

q: What blood type results from an individual having two copies of the I° allele?
e: Those with only two copies of the I° allele have neither antigen, resulting in type O blood.

q: If an individual is a heterozygote with genotype IAI°, what is their blood phenotype?
e: Individuals who are IAI° heterozygotes have blood type A because the I° allele produces no antigen.

q: Which of the following genotypes represents a heterozygous type B individual?
e: IBI° is a heterozygote that results in blood type B.

q: What terminal carbohydrate is added to the RBC receptor by the enzyme encoded by the A gene?
e: RBCs of type A contain an enzyme that adds N-acetyl galactosamine to the receptor.

q: What terminal carbohydrate does the enzyme encoded by the B gene add to RBC receptors?
e: RBCs of type B have an enzyme that adds D-galactose.

q: Why do type O red blood cells lack a terminal carbohydrate on their receptors?
o: The enzyme adds an invisible molecule
They lack the genes and enzymes to add a terminal molecule
The terminal molecule is destroyed instantly
They add both carbohydrates that cancel each other
e: RBCs of type O lack the genes and enzymes to add a terminal molecule.

q: The ABO antigens are not primary gene products but rather the products of what?
e: The ABO antigens are enzymatic reaction products of enzymes called glycosyltransferases.

q: When both alleles of a pair are fully expressed in a heterozygote, they are called:
e: When both alleles of a pair are fully expressed in a heterozygote they are called Codominants.

q: The expression of the IA and IB alleles in an individual to form blood type AB is a classic example of:
e: The ABO blood group antigens are a good example of codominance, as both IA and IB are expressed fully.

q: A mating between a homozygous type A person (IAIA) and a homozygous type B person (IBIB) will result in offspring with what blood type?
e: It would result in all heterozygous AB-type (IAIB) offspring.

q: ABO blood typing can be useful in legal contexts, primarily for which of the following?
e: The genetics of ABO antigens were once used to rule out paternity.

q: If a mother is Type O and the father is Type O, what are the possible blood types for their offspring?
o: Types A, B, AB, and O
e: According to the inheritance chart, a mating between O and O can only produce O offspring.

q: If both parents have Type AB blood, which blood type is NOT possible for their offspring?
e: Type AB parents only carry A and B alleles, so they cannot produce an offspring with Type O (which requires two O alleles).

q: Before a blood transfusion, a standard technique mixes donor blood drops with antisera. What is observed to determine blood type?
e: Drops of blood are mixed with antisera... and are then observed for the evidence of agglutination.

q: Which of the following infectious agents is NOT specifically listed in the text as a target for pre-transfusion screening?
e: The text lists HIV 1 and 2, HBV, HCV, some bacteria and parasites, but does not explicitly name Tuberculosis.

q: What is another term for a 'Crossmatch' test?
e: Crossmatch is also referred to as a Compatibility Test.

q: What is the general rule of compatibility in a crossmatch test?
o: Donor antibodies must agglutinate recipient RBCs
Donor RBC antigens must not be agglutinated by recipient antibodies
Recipient RBCs must agglutinate donor antibodies
Both blood types must be identical
e: The general rule of compatibility is that the RBC antigens of the donor must not be agglutinated by antibodies in recipient's blood.

q: Which term describes a person whose plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies?
e: A universal donor (Type O) has plasma with both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.

q: If an agglutination reaction occurs when blood is mixed with Anti-A serum but NOT with Anti-B serum, what is the ABO blood type?
e: Agglutination with Anti-A indicates the presence of the A antigen, characteristic of Type A blood.

q: If a person has a heterozygous genotype for blood type A, which alleles were inherited from their parents?
e: A heterozygous type A individual carries one IA allele and one I° allele.

q: The I° allele is best described as:
e: The I° allele produces no antigen.

q: According to Table 2, what antigen does blood group A have on its RBCs?
e: Table 2 states blood group A has 'A (galactosamine)' present on RBCs.

q: When performing blood typing, what does the 'Anti-D' (or Anti-Rh) well determine?
e: Anti-D is used alongside Anti-A and Anti-B to determine the Rh factor (positive or negative).

q: Which blood type has erythrocytes with neither type A nor type B surface antigens?
e: Type O has erythrocytes with neither type A nor type B surface antigens.

q: If a mother is Type A and the father is Type O, which of the following is a possible blood type for their child?
e: If the mother is heterozygous (IAI°), she can pass the I° allele, resulting in a Type O child (I°I°).
